segments.text: You can greet, introduce yourself, and ask how someone is. Time to leave gracefully. The final, plainest parting is adiós — and, like the English goodbye, it's a tiny prayer worn smooth.
diphthong-io — the -iós is one glide, ee-OHS: ah-DYOHS, stress on the end (that's what the accent on ó marks — remember the acute-accent lesson).

adiós is a + Dios — "to God." It's the front half of an old blessing, a Dios te encomiendo, "I commend you to God" — said to someone setting off, when a journey was dangerous and you left them in God's keeping.
Every Romance sister kept the same farewell-prayer:

utterances: language: Spanish. goodbye: adiós. literally: "to God".
language: French. goodbye: adieu. literally: "to God" (à Dieu).
language: Italian. goodbye: addio. literally: "to God".
language: Portuguese. goodbye: adeus. literally: "to God".

segments.text: And English is doing the exact same thing without telling you: goodbye is a crushed-down "God be with ye." So adiós and goodbye are, at heart, the same sentence — a blessing for the road.
Dios ("God") from Latin Deus — the Deus of English deity, divine, adieu, and (via Greek Zeus, same root) the whole sky-god family.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: adiós is a final goodbye

segments.text: adiós leans toward a longer parting — you won't see them soon, or it's the end of the day. For "see you later / tomorrow," Spanish reaches for hasta …, which the rest of this chapter is about — and hasta has a surprising origin.

segments.instruction: adiós / adieu / addio / adeus — four "to God" farewells
segments.source: [YOU SAY: adiós / adieu / addio / adeus — four "to God" farewells]

segments.instruction: English "goodbye" = "God be with ye" — the same prayer
segments.source: [YOU SAY: English "goodbye" = "God be with ye" — the same prayer]

segments.text: What two words hide inside adiós? (a + Dios — "to God.") What English goodbye is built the same way? (Goodbye from "God be with ye.") Is adiós for a quick "see you soon"? (No — it's the longer/final parting; hasta … comes next.) Next: hasta, and a word Spain borrowed from Arabic.

Spanish says "see you later" as hasta luego — literally "until later." So the key word is hasta, "until." And hasta carries the single most important fact about Spanish's history: for nearly 800 years, much of Spain spoke Arabic.
silent-h — Spanish h is always silent: hasta = AHS-tah (no breath on the h at all). Stress the front.

hasta comes from Arabic ḥattā, “until, up to.” From 711 CE, Muslim armies ruled much of the Iberian Peninsula — al-Andalus — and Arabic was the language of government, science, and poetry there for centuries, until.
Spanish absorbed roughly four thousand Arabic words in that time — more of its vocabulary than from any source except Latin itself.
Most of those loans are nouns, and you can spot a huge number by the frozen Arabic article al- ("the") fused onto the front:
almohada (pillow), alcázar (fortress), alcalde (mayor), alfombra (rug), aduana (customs), álgebra, alcohol.
azúcar (sugar), aceite (oil), naranja (orange).

But hasta is rare and special: it is a function word — a preposition, part of the grammatical skeleton. Languages borrow nouns easily and grammar words almost never — so an Arabic preposition surviving in everyday Spanish shows how deep, how intimate, those centuries of contact were. (Its Latin rival ad "to"/usque "up to" simply lost.) You say a piece of al-Andalus every time you say goodbye.

segments.instruction: "hasta" then Arabic ḥattā — the same word, 1,300 years apart
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "hasta" then Arabic *ḥattā* — the same word, 1,300 years apart]

segments.text: What language is hasta from, and what does it mean? (Arabic ḥattā — "until.") Why is it remarkable that Spanish borrowed it? (It's a function word / preposition — languages almost never borrow those; it shows how deep the Arabic centuries went.) How do you spot many Arabic nouns in Spanish? (The frozen al- article: almohada, azúcar, álgebra.)

lessons.title: hasta aquí / hasta la noche — point to the limit
lessons.gloss: hasta points to an endpoint in space or time

segments.text: You know hasta means “until” or “up to.” Give that small word one spatial endpoint and one temporal endpoint, using only one new word.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: endpoints in space and time

segments.text: Aquí means here. Put it after hasta:
hasta aquí — up to here.
For a time endpoint, reuse la noche, “the night,” which you already have:
hasta la noche — until the night / until tonight.
The same preposition points to a place or the end of a stretch of time. The next lessons will place new time words after it one at a time.
What does hasta point to? (An endpoint.) Give one spatial and one temporal example. (Hasta aquí; hasta la noche.) What is the only new lexical item? (Aquí, “here.”)
One farewell that is final, and one word that opens all the others. Nothing new in this lesson — only what you already have.
Adiós — meant, and a little final. Hasta — "until," and it is waiting for what comes next.
You can close a conversation, and you have the word every softer goodbye is built from.
